key_insight: Language models should not be trusted to reliably attribute or situate knowledge on their own; doing so requires explicit provenance, contextual metadata, and system designs that separate generation from source-tracking.
problem_solved: Addresses the risk that LLMs produce plausible but ungrounded or misattributed claims, leaving users unable to verify origin, context, or applicability of generated knowledge.
method: Critical analysis and empirical demonstrations highlighting failure modes where LMs misattribute, omit, or decontextualize sources.
Comparison of model-generated outputs with ground-truth provenance and contextual metadata to show gaps in reliable attribution.
Recommendations for system-level practices (external retrieval, provenance tracking, human-in-the-loop auditing) to ensure verifiable and situated knowledge.
impact: Prompts practitioners to stop treating generation as an implicit source of truth and to build architectures and workflows that enforce provenance, context, and accountability—reducing misinformation, legal risk, and misuse in deployed AI systems.
visual_elements: Flowchart contrasting a plain LLM pipeline (generation only) versus a provenance-aware pipeline (retrieval → citation → generation → human review).
Before/after examples: side-by-side model output that hallucinates a source vs. a verified output with proper citation and context.
Bar chart or schematic summarizing common failure modes (misattribution, decontextualization, omission) and their relative frequency or severity.
Checklist/infographic of recommended engineering and governance practices (external provenance store, logging, audits, user-facing indicators).
paper_title: Attributing and situating knowledge cannot be left to language models
